Expiration actions define when objects\\nare\\nremoved. The effect of these actions depends on the versioning state of your bucket\\nand\\nobjects. Transitions and expirations are asynchronous operations. Your S3 costs, however,\\nare updated as though transitions and expirations were immediate.\\n\\nAmazon S3 has a list of supported lifecycle transitions between storage classes. Additionally, you can\\nchange the default transition behavior so that objects smaller than 128 KB will transition\\nto S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive. To do this, use the\\noptional `x-amz-transition-object-size-minimum-default` header in a PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration request.\\n\\nThe effects of expiration actions are permanent. To prevent accidental deletion, we\\nrecommend that you take precautions, such as enabling S3 Versioning, S3 Object Lock, multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete, or S3 Replication.\\n\\nUnder **Review transition and expiration actions**, you can also review how the specified actions work on the lifecycle of\\ncurrent and noncurrent versions of objects.\\n\\nThere are per-request transition charges to move data into any supported S3 storage\\nclass\\nand charges to store the transitioned objects in the storage class. To do so, your lifecycle\\nconfiguration must include current versions, noncurrent versions, delete markers,\\nand\\nincomplete multipart uploads.\\n\\nAmazon S3 also supports a bucket lifecycle rule to stop multipart uploads that don't\\nfinish\\nwithin a specified number of days after being initiated. An expired object delete marker occurs when all object versions are\\n deleted, and only a single delete marker remains. If you selected this option in\\n your lifecycle rule, an expired object delete marker will be deleted.\\n* You can also see if your lifecycle rule deletes incomplete multipart uploads after\\n a specified number of days\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-rule-view-page.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Cost optimization in analytics services\",\"context\":\"##### Amazon S3 lifecycle policies\\n\\nA\\nlifecycle\\npolicy automatically move objects in your bucket from\\none storage class to another. Regular data cleanup into\\ndistinct storage classes is crucial in the big data\\nprocessing. Data lakes have different data layers like\\nsource, raw, process, and business data. Once the data is\\nprocessed, the source and raw data layers are rarely\\naccessed. As a result, transitioning them to infrequent and\\narchive storage class could save money. You can avoid the\\nmanual cleanup process with lifecycle policies to save on\\ncosts.\\n\\nCreate a lifecycle rule to automatically transition your\\nobjects to Standard-IA storage class, archive them to\\nGlacier storage class, and remove them after a specified\\nperiod.\\n\\nLifecycle transition costs are directly proportional to the\\nnumber of objects transitioned, so reduce the number of\\nobjects by aggregating or zipping and compressing them\\nbefore moving them to archive tiers. Apply life cycle\\npolicies to the source, staging, and other data sets that\\nare processed and would no longer be needed.\\n\\nCreate lifecycle policies to clean up incomplete multipart\\nuploads. Also, you can organize data to make life cycle\\npolicies simpler and more effective. For example, keep all\\nsource data under one prefix so you can have a single\\nlifecycle policy for all the source data sets rather than\\none for each source prefix. In addition, use lifecycle\\npolicies to delete many objects to avoid S3 API costs.\\nFinally, if your bucket is versioned, ensure there is a rule\\naction for both current and non-current objects to either\\ntransition or expire\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/cost-modeling-data-lakes/cost-optimization-in-analytics-services.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Look up S3 Lifecycle cost-saving documentation"}

{"id": "bb1ae508-dfb2-4c9a-9bf3-587d83261a72", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Lifecycle rules save money by moving data to cheaper storage classes as it ages and by deleting data you no longer need. These are the levers that usually matter most.

## 1. Transition objects to cheaper storage classes
Transition actions move objects after a set number of days since creation. A typical ladder looks like this:
- **S3 Standard** for hot data.
- **Standard-IA** or **One Zone-IA** after about 30 days, for data you read rarely but still need quickly.
- **Glacier Instant, Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive** after 90 days or more, for archives.

If you can't predict access patterns, **S3 Intelligent-Tiering** moves objects between tiers for you. You can also use a lifecycle rule to move objects into it.

## 2. Expire data you don't need
- Add an **expiration** action for logs, temp files, build artifacts and raw or staging data. For example, delete after 90 days.
- Expiration is permanent. On important buckets, enable versioning, Object Lock, MFA delete or replication first.

## 3. Clean up hidden costs
These are often the biggest savings:
- **Abort incomplete multipart uploads** after 7 days. These leftover parts are billed but never show up as normal objects.
- **Expire noncurrent versions** on versioned buckets, for example after 30 days. You can also keep only the newest N noncurrent versions. Without this rule, old versions accumulate indefinitely.
- **Remove expired object delete markers.**
- Make sure versioned buckets have actions for both current and noncurrent versions.

## 4. Watch for gotchas
- **Small objects:** by default, objects under 128 KB aren't transitioned. Transition requests are billed per object, so moving millions of tiny objects can cost more than it saves. Aggregate or compress them first, or use an object size filter.
- **Minimum storage durations:** IA and Glacier classes bill for a minimum period (30 days for Standard-IA, longer for Glacier tiers). Deleting or transitioning an object before that period still charges you for the full minimum. Don't use short expiry windows on these classes.
- **Retrieval fees:** IA and archive classes charge to read data back. Don't archive anything you access often.
- **Transition request charges:** each transition costs a small fee per object, so the savings come from storing large volumes for a long time.
- Transitions and expirations run asynchronously, but your bill is calculated as if they happened immediately.

## 5. Scope rules sensibly
- Use prefix, tag or object-size filters to target specific data. You can have up to 1,000 rules per bucket.
- Keep data of the same age and type under one prefix, so one rule covers it instead of many.

## Example rule (JSON)
```json
{
  "Rules": [{
    "ID": "logs-tiering",
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
    "Transitions": [
      { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
      { "Days": 90, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
    ],
    "Expiration": { "Days": 365 },
    "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30 },
    "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
  }]
}
```

## Where to start
1. Use **S3 Storage Lens** or **Storage Class Analysis** to see which buckets and prefixes are large and how often they're accessed.
2. Roll out the safe rules first: abort incomplete multipart uploads and expire noncurrent versions.
3. Then add transitions and expirations based on the access data.

I can review your buckets and find the ones missing these rules, such as no multipart cleanup or no noncurrent version expiration on versioned buckets. Tell me if you'd like that.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
